title: A Reader Thread of Its Own: Nothing Else Can Hold the Reading

questions.question: A program reads a serial port on its main thread, which sometimes does something slow for longer than the buffer lasts. What is lost?
options: Whatever the device sends after the buffer fills, with no error reported to the program
The oldest bytes, with an exception
questions.explanation: The buffer keeps what it has and drops what arrives. Measured, a 900 ms stall cost 628 of 1000 frames.

questions.question: The reader thread's longest gap between looks at the port was 0.8 ms against a budget of 372 ms. What does that number show?
options: The budget can only be spent by code inside the reader's loop, and that loop has no slow work in it
questions.explanation: Moving the reading to a thread of its own changes who can spend the budget. Exposing the longest gap lets you see how much of it has been.

questions.question: Why is the thread declared as the last member of LinkReader?
options: It starts after everything it uses exists, and the compiler joins it before any of that is destroyed, because members are destroyed in reverse order
Threads must be last in every class
questions.explanation: A thread declared first starts before the queue and the link exist. Declared last, its start and its join are both on the right side of everything it touches.

questions.question: With every read failing, the reader made 355 attempts in 200 ms. Why not millions?
options: It rests after a failure as well as after nothing waiting, so a dead cable does not cost a core
questions.explanation: A loop that rests only when nothing was waiting has a branch with no rest in it. A failing port takes that branch.

questions.question: What does latest() give you that a plain shared struct does not?
options: A whole message or a retry, never the first half of one write and the second half of the next, which a plain struct copied across threads can produce and which is a data race
questions.explanation: A sixty four byte struct is not copied in one step. A Seqlock lets the reader detect that a write overlapped and try again, without ever blocking the writer.

questions.question: The queue behind pop() is full and nobody is taking messages. What happens, and why is it done that way?
options: The reader blocks until there is room
New messages are dropped and counted, so the reader's budget is never spent waiting and a slow consumer shows up as a number
questions.explanation: A reader that blocks on its own queue is the main thread's problem again. Dropping and counting keeps the reader on time and makes the consumer's slowness visible.
